When I retired from swimming at twenty, the hardest thing was not the training I had lost. It was the shape of the day. For eight years somebody else had decided what came first and what came next, and the moment that disappeared, I discovered I had no idea how to decide it myself. I would sit down to study and, before I knew it, three hours had gone and nothing had happened. What fixed it was embarrassingly small. I gave every task a beginning and an end, so that I always knew which part of the day I was in. As soon as one task finished, I stood up, even for one minute. My mind needed a whistle, the way it always had in the pool. Once I gave it one, the days started to feel like days again.

One of the most useful questions I ask students is not what will you do. It is what will have happened by the time. By the time the exam is over, what will you have done? By the time you start university, what will you have stopped doing? The question works because it makes you plan backwards. Instead of starting from today and hoping the year arranges itself, you start from the end and ask what has to come first. Most students I talk to are surprised by how short the answer is. As long as three or four things happen in the right order, the rest tends to fall into place. The trouble is never the size of the plan. It is the sequence, and almost nobody writes the sequence down.
